body.x: Drones and other unmanned platforms used in defense and security need video that stays low-latency in low light and at night, and defense customers increasingly ask suppliers to show transparent, resilient supply chains.
Luna Robotics' answer is to supply the vision layer rather than a complete drone.

UAB Luna Robotics, a defense technology company founded in 2024 in Vilnius, Lithuania, is led by CEO Elvinas Kukys. It is exhibiting at KES 2026 with Luna Vision camera systems for FPV drones, interceptor drones, unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) and other unmanned platforms, and says it wants to build partnerships with Korean drone makers, defense companies and system integrators.

Luna Vision pairs purpose-built camera hardware with software-enhanced image processing at the edge, which the company says supports low-latency video and better visibility in daylight, low-light and night conditions. The system also handles functions such as object detection and tracking and can work with external sensors such as radar. Because it is platform-agnostic, manufacturers can integrate it into their own platforms, and Luna Robotics says it develops the critical electronics and software without Chinese-origin components.

The company says it moved from product development to serial production in under two years and had shipped more than 2,900 camera systems by the second quarter of 2026, used by Lithuanian and Ukrainian defense users. In a 2026 test campaign with Lithuanian defense partners, an interceptor platform using its technology scored eight hits in eight attempts against a flying drone target, including in conditions where satellite navigation was denied. Luna Robotics holds a NATO Stock Number and an NCAGE code and is expanding cooperation with defense manufacturers and system integrators in Europe and the United States.

Luna Robotics supplies customers in Lithuania and exports to Ukraine. Its priority markets are the United States, South Korea and NATO-aligned European countries, where it plans to integrate its vision technology into existing platforms rather than compete with local manufacturers. In South Korea, it is seeking long-term OEM and technology-integration partnerships with manufacturers serving domestic and export markets.

Next, the company plans to increase production capacity, deepen OEM integration, develop thermal and multi-sensor vision systems and build dedicated solutions for interceptor drones, UGVs and unmanned surface vehicles (USVs). It cites certification and qualification requirements, long procurement cycles, export-control compliance and finding trusted local partners as the main challenges in defense exports.

KES 2026, the 57th Korea Electronics Show, runs Oct. 13 to Oct. 16 at COEX Halls A and B in Seoul. Alongside the co-located XR & Spatial Computing Show, the event features X-SPACE 2026, a special exhibition covering digital twins, industrial XR, spatial intelligence, XR devices and spatial computing platforms. The Innovation Awards ceremony takes place on Oct. 13.
